title: A Cosy Tent in Edison Became New Jersey's Most Unlikely Hindi Theatre
excerpt: Playwright Ashok Vyas and the Heramba Art and Culture Center staged dramatic readings of three mystical natak — drawing two dozen guests into a world where divine coincidence trumps Silicon Valley logic
body:
On a mild Friday afternoon on May 9, a backyard tent in Edison, New Jersey, became the most improbable theatre in the Indian diaspora. No proscenium stage, no ticketed audience, no intermission chai counter — just two dozen invited guests, folding chairs, and three original Hindi plays performed as dramatic readings under the banner "Beyond Understanding."

The event marked the soft launch of the **Heramba Art and Culture Center**, a New York-based initiative that has quietly operated for years through its YouTube channel HerambaStudio, producing dharmic, spiritual and mental-health programming. Now, in collaboration with **Prayog Natya Sanstha**, it stepped into live performance — and the result felt less like theatre and more like a spiritual living-room experiment.

## Three Plays, One Thread

The plays were written by **Ashok Vyas**, a poet, Hindu priest and veteran television host with over 25 years on **ITV Gold**, the longest-running South Asian TV network in the United States. The unifying theme — "Beyond Understanding" — explored the tension between rational modernity and the inexplicable pull of faith.

The first play, *Agyat Ka Bhay* (Fear of the Unknown), followed a disillusioned man teetering on suicidal thoughts whose unplanned visit to a friend's home becomes a turning point through a chain of seemingly divine manifestations — including the spontaneous formation of a Shivalinga in snow and the appearance of Lord Krishna's form on household tiles. Host **Abhishek Mishra** and his wife **Namita** played themselves in the reading, blurring the boundary between drama and testimony.

*Mystical Chai*, the second piece, pivoted to the age of social media and artificial intelligence. A young New Jersey devotee of the Mother Goddess finds himself at the centre of events that probe how digital-age scepticism coexists with unshakeable devotion — and how, as Vyas frames it, "what we deem impossible can become possible by divine will."

The final play, *Chief Controller*, broadened the canvas further. Its protagonists are founders of a technology company with revenues exceeding four billion dollars — one of whom attributes his success to the protection of **Gala Bhomiya ji**, a *lok devta* (folk deity) from Rajasthan. The play's closing argument — that exponential technological growth demands a proactive defence of human sensitivity — drew the warmest response from the audience.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Hindi-language theatre in America has always been a labour of love, sustained by community associations from New Brunswick to the Bay Area. Events like the **South Asian Theater Festival** (now in its 19th year) and **Natya Darpan**, a multilingual short-play festival run by the Indian Heritage and Cultural Association of New Jersey, have built real audiences. But intimate readings like this one — spiritual, vernacular, unhurried — fill a different gap.

For NRIs whose connection to Hindi extends beyond Bollywood, these gatherings are acts of cultural maintenance. Vyas's plays engage a register that rarely surfaces in diaspora entertainment: Vedantic philosophy delivered through the conventions of *natak*, aimed at professionals who code by day and question karma by night.

Among the guests were **Parveen Chopra**, founder of ALotusInTheMud.com; yoga teacher **Vijay Trivedi**; **Pradeep Agarwal** of Vishwa Hindi Nyas; and **Dr Om Sharma**, founder of the GICA Hanuman Mandir. Vineeta Khanna of the Orator Academy performed a bhajan of Sant Kabir and a ghazal. Several guests later visited the Mishra residence to see what many described as miraculous divine imprints — bringing the afternoon's theme to life in a deeply personal way.

## What's Next

The Heramba Art and Culture Center plans to stage further readings across the tri-state area. For a community that can fill a stadium for a Diljit Dosanjh concert but struggles to find fifty people for a Hindi play, the Centre's bet is clear: start small, start soulful, and let the work speak for itself.
